4721.tone: Naorem 2009: 'Being a Tibeto-Burman language, Simte also has the tonal system. There are two tones in Simte, viz. (a) falling tone /ˋ/ and (b) level tone /ˉ/. Falling tone is marked and level tone is not marked.'; 'In this language, tones are limited although some words do have.' Minimal pairs, level vs falling, read from (p. 49): ɟu 'rat'/ɟù 'wine', ni 'aunt'/nǐ 'day', si 'die'/sǐ 'blood', ŋa 'five'/ŋà 'fish', ləy 'tongue'/lə̀y 'bridge', si-al 'fox'/sǐal 'mithun', la 'take'/là 'song', ha 'month'/hà 'teeth'; (p. 50): məy 'fire'/mə̀y 'tail', sun 'mid-day'/sùn 'mourn', thəw 'fat'/thə̀w 'rise', peh 'kick'/pèh 'broad', kəy 'I'/kə̀y 'bite', lam 'dance'/làm 'wealth', bel 'pot'/bèl 'help', gəmla 'flower'/gəmlà 'distance'. (The p. 50 glosses kəy 'I'/kə̀y 'bite' and lam 'dance'/làm 'wealth' are as printed; A's 'kay dance/bite' and 'lam -/wealth' were an scan column shift. The initial of the first pair is the voiced palatal plosive /ɟ/ of Table 3, p. 17, not /j/; A and B both wrote ju.) The words stress, accent, prominence, intonation and pitch do not occur in the chapter except in the Clark & Yallop tone definition quoted on p. 49 (nor in the Ch. I or bibliography scan). Kapginlian 2025 (Morpho Syntax of Simte, NEHU PhD, ch. 2 pp. 116-118), citing Ching 2022, instead reports 'four tones as contrast to Singh (2009) findings' -- 'Register tones: mid [ˉ] and low tone [ˋ], and two Contour tones: falling rising [ˇ] and rising falling [ˆ] (Ching, 2022, p.76)'…

4723.dq: ' shows where the accent falls: in the absence of any mark the accent falls on the penultimate syllable. [A key to wordlist citation forms; 'word' is never named and no Singa phrase-level or word-level description exists.]
4723.dloc: Johnston 1904 vol. 2, p. 901; Lusinga column pp. 993-1000; locale line p. 993. Johnston 1919 vol. 1 p. 41.
4723.prule: No Singa-specific statement exists. The only stress-related text is Johnston's volume-wide transcription key (p. 901), applying to all fifty vocabularies (Nilotic, Masai, Somali and Bantu alike): an acute marks the accented syllable, and an unmarked word is accented on the penultimate syllable. Under that convention the ~70 unmarked Lusinga items (Johnston reprints about half of Hobley's 142 filled entries) are implicitly penult-accented and one item, Mwanámtu 'child' (compound mwana + mtu), is marked antepenult. But the Lusinga list is Hobley's 1902 list reprinted (Hobley's printing has no accent marks and no pronunciation key), so the macrons and the single acute are Johnston's editorial additions to data he did not collect; the convention is not an observation about Singa.
4723.srule: Not mentioned in Johnston 1904 vol. 2 (orthography key p. 901; Lusinga vocabulary pp. 993-1000): the key supplies one accent mark per word and says nothing about secondary or rhythmic stress; Hobley 1902 pp. 92-95 and Johnston 1919 vol. 1 p. 41 are likewise silent.

4726.dq: Stress is predictable, occurring on the last syllable of the root, irrespective of suffixes. In polymorphemic complex verbs, for example, stress falls on the root-final syllable, not on the added modifier or directional (§3.1). [1987] The main stress ... occurs on the last syllable of the word nucleus, the part which carries the central meaning.

4726.prule: Stress is predictable and falls on the last syllable of the root, irrespective of suffixes; prefixes/proclitics and suffixes (modifiers, directionals, negator -tap, object markers) are unstressed. In polymorphemic complex verbs (simple root + modifier or directional suffix) stress stays on the root-final syllable, not on the added modifier or directional. Word-final only when the root is word-final.

tn.translation: On the suprasegmental level, every syllable nucleus in Nsong carries at least one tone. 4735.heavy: Not defined in the relayed passage. The rule is stated as mora-counting ('stress assignment is mora-sensitive'; 'stress is assigned on the penultimate voiced mora'), with 'voiceless moras being treated as extrametrical'. Which syllables are bimoraic (long vowels, diphthongs, codas or geminates) is not said.
4735.dflt: Not stated. If every syllable is a single voiced mora the penultimate mora is the penultimate syllable; if the final vowel is devoiced (extrametrical) the penultimate voiced mora is the antepenultimate syllable, while high pitch stays on the penultimate syllable.
4735.prule: Hypothesis (Rehg 1993: 32, relayed by Vita 2020: 19): primary stress on the penultimate voiced mora, counting from the right edge; voiceless (devoiced word-final) moras are extrametrical and do not count, so a word with a devoiced final vowel is stressed one mora further left than the surface penult. High pitch (level 3 of the 231 contour) sits on the penultimate syllable, so stress and pitch peak can fall apart when the final vowel is devoiced.

dfl.q: Within the domain of a bisyllabic word stem, stress falls on the first syllable, for example: 'lakʷan "child" If a derivative suffix is added, however, then stress generally falls on the final syllable, for example: lakʷa'n-a child-1.SG.POSS "my child"

4738.dq: Ударение в именных частях речи и в наречиях падает на последний слог слова: estā̊ré ‘звезда’, rušán ‘светлый’, digé ‘другой’, pånjá ‘пятьдесят’, hâmišé ‘всегда’. (p. 154; 'the last syllable of the word', stated for parts of speech, with a separate word-level rule for verb forms; Christensen § 38 separately lists the unaccented clitics of the phrase.)
4738.dloc: Rastorgueva 1999: p. 154 (Sorkhei article, section 'Foneticheskie svedenija', 3rd paragraph); pp. 149-150 (belt article). Christensen 1935: p. 35 § 38.
4738.prule: Word stress on the final syllable of the word in nouns, adjectives, pronouns, numerals and adverbs (Sorkhei p. 154 categorical: 'падает на последний слог слова'; Aftari p. 165 'обычно' = usually; belt article pp. 149-150 the same rule for Sorkhei, Lasgerdi, Biyabanaki, Aftari). Syllable weight is never mentioned; the pattern is the Persian type (Christensen § 35: 'les mêmes règles que le persan'). The ezafe -e and the indefinite/unit marker -i are unstressed, so stress stays on the last stem syllable.
4738.srule: Stated only for verb forms, placed by morphology: when the main stress falls on a verbal prefix (derivational ha-, da-, du-, va-; be-/me-; negation nå-/ne-), the personal ending carries a secondary stress ('основное ударение падает на префикс, вспомогательное — на окончание': hákennìm 'we make', hákårdàm 'I made', dábåstàm, dúrizìn, váporsìn, vanǻporsìn; p. 150 vǻporsìn, békatìm, mébordàm). Christensen 1935 § 37 (first-hand): with a prefix the ending 'porte ordinairement en sourkhéī... un accent secondaire, qui peut paraître parfois presque aussi fort que l'accent du préfixe'; § 36 the preterite ending may carry a secondary accent. No secondary stress is mentioned for nouns, adjectives, pronouns, numerals or adverbs (final main stress only).

4739.dq: 'Drawling' in general is due to the absence of stress accent, and was probably a feature of West-Arabian altogether (cf. § 10 p).
4739.prule: No stress rule. Rabin infers that Himyaritic, like West-Arabian generally but more markedly, lacked an expiratory (stress) accent; the inference rests on al-Hamdānī's tenth-century characterisation of Himyaritic speech as 'halting' (muʿaqqad) and 'drawling' (yajurrūna fī kalāmihim), which Rabin equates with absence of stress accent. No stress position is stated or derivable.
4739.srule: Not mentioned in Rabin 1951 (ch. 5 §5 l-o, pp. 49-50, and ch. 10 §10 l-q, pp. 102-105, read in full): Rabin denies an expiratory (stress) accent for West-Arabian and Himyaritic altogether and never discusses secondary or rhythmic stress.
4739.quote: We get a more instructive indication in the term muʿaqqad 'halting' with which Hamdānī describes both Himyaritic itself and the dialects influenced by it. It seems that he means the same when he says that the people of Sarw Ḥimyar 'drawl' (yajurrūna fī kalāmihim). 'Drawling' in general is due to the absence of stress accent, and was probably a feature of West-Arabian altogether (cf. § 10 p). But South-Arabian must have had a drawling of a much more pronounced character, which produced the two-peak syllables of Minaean and other dialects (cf. Rhodokanakis, Studien, i, 12–56). It is this featur…
4739.loc: Ch. 5 'Himyar', §5 n, p. 49 (dli.ernet.103575); cross-references ch. 10 'Hijaz: the vowels', §10 m-p, pp. 102-105; the two p. 104 sentences quoted (§10 n and the opening sentence of §10 p, which sits at the foot of p. 104) are on p. 121
4739.idn: 'Himyaritic' (the language of Himyar) as described by al-Hamdani for tenth-century highland Yemen: pure 'halting' Himyaritic in the central mountain area around San'a' and the southern Sarat (Rabin ch. 5, pp. 42-45); data: No fieldwork: a philological study of medieval Arabic sources, chiefly al-Hamdani (d. 334/946)…
4739.exq_: It cannot be sufficiently stressed that these are merely impressionist terms: we are moving on ground that has not been satisfactorily investigated by modern phonetics. (pp. 102-103)
4739.tone: Rabin's frame (§10 m, p. 102) opposes an 'expiratory or stress accent' (English, German, Russian; in Semitic Hebrew, Aramaic; Syrian Arabic) to 'the opposite, non-expiratory type of accent' (French, American English, Indian languages, Amharic) in which 'slight expiratory prominence is lent to syllables by factors such as emphasis and sentence rhythm'; he places West-Arabian and, a fortiori, Himyaritic in the second type. He does not claim tone or a pitch accent for Himyaritic.
4739.sec_quote: It seems thus pretty well established that West-Arabian did not possess an expiratory stress.
